strengths: The interactive formulation is practically meaningful: unifying initial UI-to-code generation, iterative polishing from rendered feedback, and targeted editing better reflects real front-end workflows than one-shot generation.

UI2CodeN-9B reports large, consistent gains over comparably sized open models across Design2Code, Flame-React-Eval, Web2Code, and the proposed real-world benchmark; the reported results are competitive with much larger proprietary systems.
The paper studies a substantial training pipeline spanning continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO, and provides useful ablations on reward design and inclusion of real webpages.

The comparator and round-robin verifier are sensible attempts to reduce calibration drift in VLM-based rewards. Table 3 suggests that these refinements improve polishing performance over the vanilla verifier.
Presentation is generally clear, and the qualitative examples support the claim that the model can reproduce diverse layouts and perform instruction-based edits.
weaknesses: The central performance claims rely almost entirely on proprietary VLM judges without human validation. UI-to-code success is defined by an o4-mini score exceeding an arbitrary threshold of 80, while polishing is judged by Gemini-2.5-Pro. The paper reports no judge-human agreement, evaluator variance, order-randomization test, confidence intervals, or repeated trials. Reward ablations showing that one learned judge outperforms CLIP do not establish that the evaluation judges are reliable.

The polishing metric is particularly weak: it records only whether output C is judged better than B, treating a negligible improvement like a major one and providing no absolute-fidelity result. The fixed presentation order also permits position bias, and the provenance and difficulty of the initial renderings in UIPolish-Bench are insufficiently specified. The claim that 50% constitutes a chance threshold is not justified for this non-random comparison task.

UI editing is advertised as one of the model's three central capabilities, but it receives no quantitative evaluation, baselines, or instruction-following assessment; only selected qualitative examples are shown. Thus a major contribution is unsupported.

Potential train-test contamination is not addressed. Pretraining uses roughly 10 million crawled webpages plus WebSight and WebCode2M, while evaluation includes public real-webpage benchmarks and a newly crawled real-world set. No URL-, screenshot-, DOM-, or near-duplicate filtering against any evaluation set is described.

The evaluation omits important aspects of usable UI code: compilation/render success rates, functional behavior, responsiveness, accessibility, semantic correctness, maintainability, and security. Screenshot resemblance alone does not substantiate broad claims of executable or practically useful front-end generation.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The promised code/model URL is blank, the new datasets and outputs are not supplied, the exact base checkpoint is described only as an 'early checkpoint,' and key details are missing for data filtering, deduplication, verifier fine-tuning, GRPO configuration, decoding, baseline prompting, rendering environment, and commercial evaluator versions.

Some reported results are internally difficult to reconcile. For example, UI2CodeN-SFT scores 79.3 on Design2Code in Table 1 but 72.3 in Table 3 despite the ablation being described as starting from the SFT checkpoint; the differing protocol or checkpoint is not explained. No uncertainty or multi-seed evidence accompanies the relatively small ablation differences.

The originality claims are overstated. Iterative rendering-and-revision and agentic UI generation already appear in the cited literature; the main novelty is better characterized as training a unified model for this workflow and introducing a particular VLM-verifier recipe, rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

There is no dedicated limitations or ethics discussion. Crawling approximately 10 million webpages raises unresolved copyright, licensing, privacy, consent, and benchmark-contamination issues. The paper also does not discuss risks from generated executable web code, such as unsafe scripts, deceptive interface replication, or accessibility failures. These omissions matter given the scale and intended deployment setting.

strengths: Significance: UI-to-code is practically important, and jointly supporting initial generation, targeted editing, and iterative screenshot-conditioned polishing is a useful system objective.

Soundness: The three-stage pipeline is broadly sensible: large-scale continual pretraining, task-specific supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning using rendered visual feedback. The reported SFT-to-RL gains are substantial.

Evaluation breadth: The paper compares against numerous open- and closed-source VLMs on several public benchmarks, two new benchmarks, and multiple UI-related tasks. Reward-design and real-versus-synthetic-data ablations provide some useful evidence.
Presentation: The high-level method is easy to follow, and the appendix supplies reward algorithms, judge prompts, training hyperparameters, and readable qualitative examples.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline results depend almost entirely on unvalidated VLM-as-judge metrics. Public benchmarks are evaluated using an o4-mini score threshold of 80 rather than their established metrics, with no human correlation study, judge reliability analysis, repeated judging, or justification for the threshold. UI polishing is judged by Gemini-2.5-Pro using merely whether C is scored above B, so arbitrarily small or noisy score differences count as success.

Soundness: The new UI2Code-Real and UIPolish benchmarks are severely underdocumented. The paper gives little beyond sample counts and broad provenance; it omits sampling criteria, source lists, deduplication, licenses, difficulty characterization, and quality-control procedures. Since training includes roughly 10M crawled webpages plus Mind2Web and public UI datasets, train-test contamination is a serious unresolved concern.

Soundness: UI editing is advertised as one of three central capabilities but receives no quantitative evaluation. Its support consists only of selected qualitative examples, so a major claimed contribution is not established.

Experimental evidence: The ablations do not isolate the contributions of continual pretraining, SFT data construction, RL, model initialization, or data scale. Reward ablations cover only two public benchmarks, use small self-created test sets elsewhere, provide no confidence intervals or significance tests, and show an unexplained Design2Code SFT discrepancy between Table 1 (79.3) and Table 3 (72.3).

Evaluation fairness and reproducibility: Baseline prompts, token budgets, decoding settings, retry policies, rendering environment, and exact proprietary-model versions are not adequately specified. Specialized prior systems discussed in related work are absent from the main comparison. Consequently, it is unclear whether gains reflect model quality or unequal inference protocols.

Reproducibility: Despite claiming a full training recipe and open sourcing, the manuscript's availability URL is blank. Essential details remain missing, including architecture changes relative to the early GLM-4.1V checkpoint, data mixture proportions, preprocessing and filtering rules, optimizer settings, compute budget, checkpoint selection, inference prompts, and benchmark artifacts.

Originality: Iteratively rendering code and feeding screenshots back for refinement is intuitive and overlaps substantially with prior agent-style UI-generation workflows cited by the paper. The manuscript overstates this as a fundamentally new paradigm without carefully distinguishing it from existing iterative visual-feedback systems.

Test-time scaling is demonstrated only on the authors' small, potentially contaminated benchmarks, without uncertainty estimates or equal-compute comparisons such as best-of-N sampling. The 66-to-74 improvement on 115 real examples does not by itself establish a general scaling property.

Limitations and ethics: There is no meaningful limitations or research-ethics discussion. Crawling millions of webpages raises copyright, licensing, privacy, consent, and robots-policy questions, while UI cloning can facilitate impersonation or deceptive interfaces. The paper also does not discuss reliance on proprietary teachers and judges, evaluation bias, computational cost, or failure modes.

Presentation contains multiple overclaims, including calling the reward study “thorough,” asserting that sub-50% polishing accuracy means models lack genuine capability, and claiming human-aligned evaluation without presenting human evidence. These weaken confidence in an otherwise readable manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem and presents a coherent interactive formulation combining UI-to-code generation, iterative polishing, and targeted editing. Iterative rendering feedback is well motivated by the realities of frontend development.

The proposed 9B model delivers strong results across several public benchmarks. In Table 1, the RL model substantially outperforms prior open-source models and is competitive with, or better than, much larger proprietary systems on most reported tasks.

The three-stage training recipe is a meaningful systems contribution: large-scale continual pretraining, task-specific supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning directly against rendered outputs address complementary aspects of the problem.

The reward-design study is useful. Table 3 shows that naive CLIP optimization degrades performance, while the VLM comparator and round-robin ranking improve polishing results, providing actionable evidence about verifier design.

The test-time scaling result is promising: Table 2 reports consistent improvement on real webpages from 66.0 at one round to 74.0 at five rounds. The qualitative examples also show convincing fidelity across varied layouts.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and unusually forthcoming about prompts and reward algorithms in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies almost entirely on proprietary VLM judges: o4-mini with an author-selected score threshold of 80 for UI-to-code and Gemini-2.5-Pro for polishing. The paper provides no human evaluation, judge-agreement study, sensitivity analysis for the threshold, repeated judging, or validation that these metrics reliably rank close renderings. Consequently, the large headline gains are less secure than the tables suggest.

Functional correctness is not evaluated. Screenshot similarity cannot establish that generated interfaces have correct interactions, responsive behavior, accessibility, valid code, or maintainability. Claims about practical UI development should therefore be narrowed.

UI editing is presented as one of the model's three defining capabilities, but it receives only qualitative examples in Figures 7–8 and no quantitative benchmark, baseline comparison, or instruction-following assessment.

The new UI2Code-Real and UIPolish benchmarks are underspecified. The manuscript gives their sizes but little information about source selection, licenses, difficulty distribution, deduplication, initial-code construction, or possible overlap with the roughly 10M crawled pretraining pages. This leaves contamination and benchmark-selection concerns unresolved.

Some results are difficult to reconcile. For example, the SFT Design2Code score is 79.3 in Table 1 but 72.3 in Table 3, while UI2Code-Real is 76.5 in Table 1 but the one-round result is 66.0 in Table 2. Different ablation budgets or checkpoints may explain this, but the manuscript does not make the distinctions sufficiently explicit.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: the stated code/model availability line has no URL, the base model is described only as an unspecified early checkpoint, and important details such as decoding settings, rendering environment, inference prompts, data filtering, verifier-training data, and random seeds are missing. Reproduction also depends on proprietary models used for data generation and evaluation.

The ablations isolate reward variants and real-world RL data, but do not establish the contribution of continual pretraining, the 10M crawled corpus, individual SFT tasks, or joint versus separate RL. Statistical uncertainty is absent despite small custom test sets of 100–115 examples.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations and ethics discussion. Large-scale webpage crawling raises copyright, licensing, privacy, and memorization concerns; synthetic reasoning traces and proprietary judges introduce biases; and generated frontend code creates security and accessibility risks. These issues should be explicitly addressed.

Several broad claims are overstated. Calling the formulation a fundamentally new paradigm discounts prior iterative or agentic refinement systems, and the conclusion's claim of surpassing Claude and Gemini is not uniform across all benchmarks. Overall, the contribution is promising and useful, but the judge validation, benchmark documentation, and reproducibility gaps keep it at weak accept rather than accept.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical study is broad, covering drafting, polishing, and editing; numerous open- and closed-source baselines; component-level and embedding metrics; human evaluation; reward and training-stage ablations; repeated runs; and an efficiency breakdown. The reported gains over the SFT checkpoint are large, including 79.3 to 88.6 on Design2Code and 76.0 to 80.0 on UIPolish-Real.

Significance: Iterative rendering and refinement is practically well motivated for frontend development. A capable 9B model that competes with much larger systems could be useful, and the proposed real-world and polishing evaluations target weaknesses of existing benchmarks.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful formalization, prompts, training details, qualitative examples, and discussion of oscillations and reward hacking. It also reports negative results, such as degradation from CLIP rewards.

Originality: Unifying drafting, polishing, and editing as executable visual optimization is a useful perspective. Tournament-style relative visual feedback is a sensible application of preference-based reinforcement learning to UI generation, even if its algorithmic ingredients are largely established.
Ethics: The manuscript discusses privacy filtering, robots.txt, copyright, intended use, decontamination, and licensing rather than ignoring the risks of large-scale webpage crawling.
weaknesses: Soundness: Equation 7 does not justify the claimed optimization. Because both y and y' are i.i.d. samples from the same policy, any antisymmetric pairwise preference yields expected win probability 1/2, independent of the policy. A fixed/reference opponent or stop-gradient construction is needed. This is a central theoretical error, even though group-relative updates may still work empirically.

The method specification is internally inconsistent. The paper alternates between RVPO and VRPO; the main text describes tournament rewards for drafting, whereas Appendix A.1 says drafting uses a normalized absolute GLM-4.5V score. Appendix A.3 describes a binary comparison only against the previous rendering, while Algorithm 1 additionally performs candidate tournaments. Consequently, the exact method behind the headline results is unclear.

The strongest polishing evidence risks evaluator coupling: Gemini-2.5-Pro labels the data used to train the reward comparator, and Gemini-2.5-Pro is also the final polishing evaluator. Cross-evaluator results in Table 18 concern drafting, not polishing. Human evaluation supports drafting and editing, but no adequately reported human study directly validates the headline UIPolish benchmark comparisons.

Evaluation is narrow relative to the claims of executable UI generation. Most results reduce a VLM score to accuracy using an arbitrary threshold of 80; compilation/render success rates, functional behavior, responsiveness, accessibility, DOM/code maintainability, and statistical uncertainty for the main tables are not reported. Thus screenshot fidelity does not establish overall frontend correctness.

The iterative claims are overstated. Table 3 reports aggregate improvements without clearly specifying selection or stopping, while Table 16 shows per-round polishing accuracy fluctuating between 63.3% and 66.0%, and only 53.1% of steps improve already-good examples. Nearly half of high-quality cases can regress, yet no reliable acceptance or rollback mechanism is evaluated.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the contribution. The 10M-example crawled corpus and raw benchmark materials are not released; the starting point is an unspecified early GLM checkpoint; benchmark collection, initial-error construction, rendering environment, decoding settings, GRPO implementation details, and contamination checks are insufficiently specified. Claims that all data have permissive licenses also conflict with the later acknowledgment that crawled pages may be copyrighted and with the research-only model license.

The new benchmarks are small and underspecified: UI2Code-Real has 115 examples and UIPolish has 200, but sampling criteria, domain composition, difficulty distribution, annotation process, and exact construction of flawed initial renderings are missing. Hash-based screenshot deduplication alone is not convincing leakage protection for a model trained on massive Common Crawl-derived data and existing UI corpora.

Human-study reporting omits important details such as blinding, presentation-order randomization, annotator expertise and compensation, adjudication, and inter-annotator agreement. Model-level correlations computed over only four baselines, including Spearman 1.0, provide weak evidence of judge validity.

Originality is moderate rather than high: iterative render-and-revise systems already exist, and tournament preferences plus GRPO are standard components. The paper does not clearly isolate what RVPO contributes beyond using a stronger task-specific comparator and substantially more domain data.

Ethics treatment is welcome but mostly declarative. The paper does not provide audit statistics for PII and license filtering, memorization tests, or evidence that domain terms permit model training; withholding the underlying corpus also prevents independent verification of these claims.

The empirical scope is broad: multiple public and newly curated benchmarks, numerous open and proprietary baselines, component-level visual metrics, human comparisons, evaluator cross-checks, and repeated-run analysis are included.

Several reported gains are substantial, notably 79.3 to 88.6 on Design2Code from SFT to RL, strong results on Flame and UI2Code-Real, and large polishing improvements over general-purpose open models. The authors also isolate training stages and compare relative, absolute-VLM, and CLIP rewards.

The manuscript is generally readable and visually polished. It acknowledges polishing oscillations and reward hacking, investigates absolute-positioning frequency, and discusses privacy, licensing, intended use, and decontamination rather than concealing these limitations.
weaknesses: Soundness: the formal RVPO objective in Eq. 7 is problematic. With two i.i.d. samples from the same policy and a consistent pairwise comparator, the expected probability that one beats the other is 1/2, independent of the policy. Thus the stated objective cannot justify policy improvement. Tournament-ranked GRPO may still work heuristically, but the paper does not provide a correct objective or analysis connecting it to improvement in visual quality.

Soundness and presentation: the proposed method is specified inconsistently. The paper alternates between RVPO and VRPO; Algorithm 1 constructs tournament rewards and, for polishing, filters candidates against the previous rendering, whereas Appendix A.1 describes an absolute normalized drafting score and Appendix A.3 describes only a binary initial-versus-polished reward. It is consequently unclear which reward generated the principal results.

Evaluation validity: the central accuracy metric thresholds a proprietary VLM's subjective 0–100 score at an arbitrary value of 80, without threshold-sensitivity analysis. Sample-level human alignment is only moderate (Spearman 0.44 and Cohen's kappa 0.41). Several headline comparisons differ by only a few examples on sets of 80–115 cases, yet the main tables provide no confidence intervals or significance tests. Correlations exceeding 0.98 across only four evaluated models are also weak evidence of evaluator invariance.

The conclusions overstate the evidence. UI2CodeN does not outperform all larger closed systems: GPT-5 is higher on Design2Code, Web2Code, and real polishing, while Gemini is also higher on Design2Code. Under the independent metrics in Table 13, the method is not uniformly best. Likewise, the claim of consistently improving refinement conflicts with Table 16, where average polishing accuracy falls from 66.0 to 63.3 before partially recovering; no reliable stopping or rollback rule is evaluated.

The experiments do not establish that RVPO, rather than scale and data, is the decisive contribution. The model receives roughly 10M crawled pairs, 20M continual-pretraining samples, 80K SFT samples, and 42K RL examples. Reward ablations are limited and omit compute-matched best-of-N sampling, ordinary iterative self-refinement, established preference-learning/ranking objectives, and a GRPO baseline using the same judge information.

Significance is limited by evaluating almost exclusively screenshot resemblance. Despite claims about executable UI development, the paper does not test interaction, functional behavior, responsiveness, accessibility, maintainability, or broad code quality. The absolute-positioning ratio alone does not rule out reward hacking or structurally brittle code.

Originality is modest: iterative render-and-refine workflows and AI-judge preference optimization are established ideas, while RVPO is largely GRPO supplied with tournament-derived judge rewards. The paper offers a useful integration for UI generation, but the conceptual reframing and rank aggregation do not yet constitute a well-founded new optimization method.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the strength of the claims. Essential details are missing, including browser/viewport/font and dependency settings, baseline prompts and decoding parameters, optimizer and hardware configuration, exact PPO/GRPO implementation, benchmark construction protocols, annotation instructions and adjudication, and a concrete artifact-release link. The 10M-page corpus and raw webpages are not released, and dependence on proprietary evaluators further impedes replication.

Data governance is discussed, but the claims are insufficiently substantiated. Image-hash deduplication does not exclude URL-, template-, or code-level overlap between a massive Common Crawl-derived corpus and webpage-derived benchmarks. The paper also states that all data have permissive licenses while later acknowledging copyrighted crawled pages and withholding the raw corpus; the filtering and license-verification procedures need auditable detail.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering drafting, polishing, editing, iterative refinement, reward ablations, training-stage ablations, human studies, evaluator cross-checks, variance, and efficiency. The consistent SFT-to-RL gains across several evaluators support the practical value of visual-feedback training.

Significance: A compact 9B model is competitive with much larger systems across several benchmarks and performs especially well on Flame, UI2Code-Real, and synthetic polishing. Treating rendering as feedback is practically relevant to front-end development.

Originality: Unifying drafting, polishing, and editing as an executable-feedback loop is a useful framing. The tournament-based relative visual reward is a sensible adaptation of preference optimization to UI generation, although its ingredients are individually familiar.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished. Reproducibility and ethics: The manuscript reports dataset sizes, core hyperparameters, evaluator prompts, rendering-based protocols, and a substantive ethics discussion addressing crawling, robots.txt, PII, copyright, decontamination, and intended use.
weaknesses: Soundness: Equation 7 is problematic as written. If y and y' are i.i.d. samples from the same policy and preferences are antisymmetric, the expected probability that y beats y' is constant (approximately 1/2), independent of the policy. The implemented GRPO update can still learn because opponent samples are effectively treated as fixed, but it is not an unbiased optimization of the stated objective. A stop-gradient or reference/opponent policy and a corresponding derivation are needed.

The reward description is internally inconsistent. Appendix A.1 defines drafting reward as an absolute GLM-4.5V score, whereas the main method presents RVPO as tournament-based relative optimization; Algorithm 1 appears to perform all pairwise comparisons, while the efficiency discussion claims a tournament reduces comparisons. RVPO/VRPO naming also varies.

Several empirical inconsistencies weaken the central test-time-scaling claim. UI2Code-Real scores in Table 3 rise from 66 to 74, yet the same model reports 76.5 in Table 1 without explanation. Table 16 shows per-round polishing accuracy decreasing from 66.0 to 63.3 before recovering to 65.8, contrary to repeated claims of consistent improvement.

Evaluation depends heavily on thresholded proprietary VLM judgments, with no confidence intervals or significance tests for the principal tables. The reported Pearson correlation of 0.93 and Spearman correlation of 1.0 at model level are computed from only four baselines, and inter-annotator agreement is not reported. The 80-point threshold is insufficiently justified and may amplify small scoring differences.

Baseline comparability is hard to verify because exact prompts, decoding settings, rendering environment, retry/error-handling rules, and inference budgets are not fully specified. It is also unclear whether all baselines receive equivalent iterative feedback budgets.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the claimed open-source status: no concrete artifact link or release snapshot is provided, the 10M-example crawl cannot be redistributed, benchmark construction and deduplication procedures lack operational detail, and a research-only non-commercial license is not conventionally open source.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: the method mainly combines GRPO, VLM preference judging, and group-wise ranking. The paper should more precisely distinguish its contribution from existing iterative screenshot-to-code agents and relative/preference-based RL.

Limitations and ethics are discussed constructively, but important practical risks remain underexplored, including functional/accessibility correctness beyond screenshots, generated-code security, memorization from a large web crawl, and the auditability of copyright/PII filtering. The visual reward mainly establishes appearance, not maintainability or semantic correctness.
